cognate: Gk ὄνομα = Ved. nā́man- (*h₁nómn̥); Gk τίθημι = Ved. dhā- (*dʰeh₁- 'put'); Lat. nomen with in-dō (*en-dʰeh₁-). Recalled, not found in the lemmatized corpora (Hittite name-giving is mostly logographic there): Hitt. lāman dai- 'put a name' in narrative naming of a newborn (e.g. Song of Ullikummi). Incidentally the son word is cognate in the two anchors too: υἱεῖς ~ sūnúḥ (*suHnús).
drift_or_renewal: none in Greek/Vedic: both keep *h₁nómn̥ + *dʰeh₁-, and both in the middle voice (ἐθέμην, θέτο, τίθεσθ̓ ~ dadhé, dádhānaḥ). Latin keeps the verb only in the compound in-dere; the simplex 'nomen dare' (*deh₃- 'give') is a rival, renewed expression. In Vedic the collocation extends to a god's taking a name for fame (śrávase with nā́ma dadhé; śrávaḥ dadhiṣe nā́ma in RV 10.28.12).
shared_syntax: verb *dʰeh₁- (middle) with *h₁nómn̥ as direct object; the bearer of the name either in the dative (Greek: the sons named) or as subject (Vedic: the son took the name).
context: Name-giving in a family: Demosthenes' speaker relates how he named his four sons and his daughter after their grandfathers (ὀνόματα ... ἐθέμην; ἐθέμην ... ὄνομα in the sentences that follow); RV 1.103.4 tells how the son (Indra) put on a name for fame (sūnúḥ ... nā́ma dadhé). Homer uses the same verb for naming a newborn (Autolycus is asked to find the name to put on his grandson, Od. 19.403-6; the name his mother put, Od. 18.5), and Plautus has nomen indere repeatedly. The choice of 'put' rather than 'give' (*deh₃-, available and used in Latin nomen dare) or 'call', recurring with the identical noun in three corpus-attested branches (plus Hittite, recalled) and in the same voice in two, is not what independent invention predicts; it is an unmarked, everyday collocation in each language, i.e. inherited usage rather than poetic borrowing.

note: All 210 pivots are Attic forensic prose (Demosthenes, Hyperides); partners mostly Cato Agr., Plautus, AV, RV. Only defensible inherited collocation: name-giving *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁- (Gk ὄνομα θέσθαι ~ Ved. nā́ma dhā- ~ Lat. nomen indere). Considered and rejected: kin-term lists (father/mother/son, generic), Cato 141 Mars pater + pecua vs AV 5.24 pitā paśūnām (speculative), Catullus pater ut gnatos ~ RV pitā putram na (generic simile).
